patch.value: Assume AC. Let \(T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r\) and use the product Milnor model \(ET=(E_{S^1})^r\), \(BT=ET/T\), with right diagonal action \((e,x)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,t^{-1}\cdot x)\). For \(k\in\{\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}\), put \(A_T(k)=H^*(BT;k)\cong k[u_1,\ldots,u_r]\), where \(u_i=c_1(L_{\chi_i})\) is the degree-two class of the \(i\)th coordinate character line. For a smooth character \(\chi:T\to S^1\), set \(L_\chi=ET\times_T\mathbb C_\chi\), with the right equivalence \((e,z)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,\chi(t)^{-1}z)\). If \(\chi=\chi_{\mathbf n}\) for \(\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^r\), then \(c_1(L_\chi)=\sum_i n_i u_i\). Define \(\mathscr S_T(k)\) to consist of \(1\) and all finite products of \(c_1(L_\chi)\) for nontrivial characters \(\chi\). This is a multiplicative subset of \(A_T(k)\) with \(0\notin\mathscr S_T(k)\). For a topological space \(X\) with a continuous left \(T\)-action, set \(H_T^*(X;k)=H^*(ET\times_T X;k)\), with its \(A_T(k)\)-module structure induced by \(ET\times_T X\to BT\). For an \(A_T(k)\)-module \(N\), its localization \(\mathscr S_T(k)^{-1}N\) consists of fractions \(n/s\), with \(n\in N\), \(s\in\mathscr S_T(k)\), and \(n/s=n'/s'\) exactly when \(u(s'n-sn')=0\) for some \(u\in\mathscr S_T(k)\); addition is \((n/s)+(n'/s')=(s'n+sn')/(ss')\), and scalar multiplication is induced by the localized ring. The character-localized Borel equivariant cohomology is \(\mathscr S_T(k)^{-1}H_T^*(X;k)\). For \(r=0\), there are no nontrivial characters and \(\mathscr S_T(k)=\{1\}\).

patch.value: Let $\Gamma$ be the finite oriented boundary cycle of a square, with four edges $e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4$ and one plaquette. Use the compact matrix group $G=SU(2)=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-\overline b&\overline a\end{pmatrix}:a,b\in\mathbb C,\ |a|^2+|b|^2=1\right\}$ in its defining two-dimensional representation. Assign one link variable $U_j\in G$ to each edge and set the ordered plaquette holonomy to $U_p=U_1U_2U_3^{-1}U_4^{-1}$. The group is the unit sphere $S^3$ in the $(a,b)$ coordinates; let $\mu$ be its normalized round surface measure. For $\beta\ge0$, define the dimensionless action $S_\beta(U)=\beta\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}U_p\right)$ and partition function $Z_\beta=\int_{G^4}e^{-S_\beta(U)}\,d\mu^{\otimes4}(U)$. This finite graph integral satisfies $e^{-2\beta}\le Z_\beta\le1$, so it is finite and strictly positive. It has only four group variables and defines no continuum fields, no Wightman or Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction, and no Hamiltonian; it therefore does not solve the four-dimensional existence and mass-gap problem.

patch.value: Let $\mathbb{H}$ be the real quaternion algebra with basis $1,i,j,k$, multiplication $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$, and norm $|a+bi+cj+dk|^2=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$. A Lie group is a finite-dimensional smooth manifold with smooth multiplication and inversion; its Lie algebra is its tangent space at the identity with the bracket induced by left-invariant vector fields. Let $SU(2)$ be the group of unit quaternions and $SO(3)$ the group of linear maps of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb{H}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{i,j,k\}\cong\mathbb R^3$ preserving the Euclidean inner product and having determinant $+1$. A Lie algebra is simple if it is nonabelian and has no nonzero proper ideals. For this example, a compact simple gauge group means a compact connected Lie group with a simple Lie algebra. Its global form means the Lie group itself, including its central quotient, rather than only its Lie algebra. The kernel of a group homomorphism is the inverse image of the identity, and the center is the set of elements commuting with every group element. The map $\pi:SU(2)\to SO(3)$ defined by $\pi(q)x=qxq^{-1}$ is a surjective homomorphism with kernel $\{1,-1\}$; its differential identifies the simple Lie algebras of $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$, while the groups are distinct. Therefore, a proof of a claim quantified over every compact simple gauge group at $SU(2)$ alone does not discharge the separate $SO(3)$ case.

patch.value: For every compact connected finite-dimensional Lie group $G$ whose Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is nonabelian and has no nonzero proper Lie ideals, construct a nontrivial four-dimensional quantum Yang–Mills theory with gauge group $G$. A Lie group is a smooth manifold with smooth multiplication and inversion, and its Lie algebra is its tangent space at the identity with the bracket induced by left-invariant vector fields. A Wightman realization means a theory satisfying the Wightman axioms: it supplies a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, a unitary representation of translations and proper, orthochronous Lorentz isometries of Minkowski space $\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-,+,+,+)$, and local quantum fields as operator-valued tempered distributions on Schwartz test functions acting on a common dense invariant domain. The fields transform covariantly; gauge-invariant fields localized in regions whose points are spacelike separated, meaning $\eta(x-y,x-y)>0$, commute. Correlation functions are the vacuum expectation distributions of finite products of smeared fields. The self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ generating time translations has spectrum $\sigma(H)\subseteq[0,\infty)$, and there is a unique Poincaré-invariant vacuum vector $\Omega$ up to phase with $H\Omega=0$. Alternatively, a Euclidean construction gives Schwinger distributions, meaning Euclidean vacuum correlation distributions on $\mathbb R^4$, satisfying the Osterwalder–Schrader axioms (temperedness, Euclidean covariance, reflection positivity, permutation symmetry, and clustering) strongly enough for reconstruction of a Wightman theory. The required nontrivial gauge content includes local operator fields corresponding to gauge-invariant local polynomials in a smooth connection's curvature and its covariant derivatives, with short-distance correlations prescribed in a specified construction by asymptotic freedom (the perturbative prediction that the gauge coupling tends to zero at short distances) and perturbative renormalization. It includes a local stress-energy tensor whose charges generate spacetime translations and an operator product expansion, meaning a short-distance expansion of products of local fields in local fields. Here the curvature of a smooth local connection $A$ is $F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A\wedge A]$, and its covariant derivative on adjoint-valued forms is $D_A=d+[A,\cdot]$. The required mass gap is a finite number $\Delta>0$ such that $\sigma(H)\cap(0,\Delta)=\varnothing$, using units $c=\hbar=1$. Confinement is a separate question and is not part of this problem.
